pos: n. (words cut or written upon a monument or altar)
etymology: From the Latin inscriptio, a writing upon. The word occurs once, naming the six words cut into an Athenian altar that gave Paul his text on Mars' hill.
biblical_def: Paul had walked Athens and read its stonework, and he opened his address with what he had read: “For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you” (Acts 17:23). The altar was a hedge against oversight — if some deity had been missed, here was a stone for him. Paul does not congratulate the Athenians on their openness; he tells them their worship is ignorant and proceeds to end the ignorance. His first sentence about the God in question removes the whole premise of the shrine: “God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Acts 17:24). He grants what is true in their own poets and then states the consequence: “Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device” (Acts 17:29). And the address ends not with a philosophy but with a summons and a date: “And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Acts 17:30). The inscription was a confession of ignorance. Paul treated it as one.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inscription as something written or engraved, particularly on a monument, coin or pillar, to transmit it to posterity.
webster_full: INSCRIPTION, n. Something written or engraved, to communicate to posterity the character or actions of a person; a title or name.
INSCRIBE, v.t. To write or engrave words or characters on any substance, to be read by others.
ALTAR, n. An elevated place on which sacrifices were anciently offered to some deity.
DEVOTION, n. The state of being dedicated or consecrated; external worship; the forms of worship.
IDOLATRY, n. The worship of idols, images, or anything made by hands, or which is not God.
scriptures: Acts 17:23
For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
Acts 17:24
God that made the world and all things therein , seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands;
Acts 17:29
Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device.
Acts 17:30
And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:
corruption_summary: Paul's sermon at Athens is held up as a model of finding common ground with other faiths, when its argument is that the Athenians' worship was ignorant and their times of ignorance now ended.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 17 is the favourite proof text for a contextualising approach that treats every religion as a partial grasp of the same God, and the unknown-god altar as Paul's warm acknowledgement that the Athenians were already worshipping the true God imperfectly. That is not what he says. He says they worship ignorantly, that God is not like anything graven by art and man's device, and that the times of this ignorance are over because a command to repent has now gone out to all men everywhere. Paul quotes their poets the way a prosecutor quotes a defendant — taking a true sentence and pressing it against the practice it condemns.

The second corruption runs the other way, in churches that cite this chapter to forbid any engagement with the culture a hearer lives in. Paul plainly had walked the city, looked at its shrines, and read its poets, and he built his opening on what he found. The Reformed position keeps both: the point of contact is real because all men are made in God's image and know Him whether they confess it or not, and the point of conflict is total because what fallen men do with that knowledge is exchange the truth of God for a lie. Paul used the inscription. He did not endorse the altar.
roots_summary: Greek epigraphe (G1923), an inscription; agnostos (G57), unknown; sebasma (G4574), an object of worship; metanoeo (G3340), to repent.
roots_lines: Greek epigraphe (G1923) — a writing upon, inscription; Acts 17:23.
Greek agnostos (G57) — unknown; the god the altar was hedged for.
Greek sebasma (G4574) — an object of devotion; your devotions, which Paul beheld.
Greek agnoeo (G50) — to be ignorant; whom ye ignorantly worship.
Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to repent, change the mind; commandeth all men every where.
usage: “An altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD” — Paul's text at Athens.
“Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship” — his verdict on the shrine.
“Now commandeth all men every where to repent” — where the sermon lands.

pos: n. (arrangement; ordering — here, the ordering ministry of angels at Sinai)
etymology: From the Latin dispositio, an arranging or setting in order. Stephen uses it of how the law came to Israel — not directly into Moses' hand alone, but ranged and administered by angels.
biblical_def: The last sentence of Stephen's defence is an indictment, and it turns on how the law arrived: “Who have received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it” (Acts 7:53). The word describes an ordering or administration; the law was ranged and delivered through angelic ministry, which magnifies both its dignity and the guilt of breaking it. Stephen has just named the pattern he sees running through the whole history: “Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye” (Acts 7:51). Paul makes the same point about angelic mediation when he asks what the law was for: “Wherefore then serveth the law? It was added because of transgressions, till the seed should come to whom the promise was made; and it was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator” (Galatians 3:19). And Hebrews reasons from the arrangement to a warning: “For if the word spoken by angels was stedfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompence of reward; how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation” (Hebrews 2:2-3). Three writers, one argument: the greater the dignity of the delivery, the graver the guilt of the neglect.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines disposition as the act of disposing, or state of being disposed; arrangement; order; method of distribution.
webster_full: DISPOSITION, n. The act of disposing, or state of being disposed; arrangement; order; method of distribution.
DISPOSE, v.t. To set in order; to arrange; to place in a particular order or method.
ORDAIN, v.t. To appoint; to decree; to institute; to establish.
MEDIATOR, n. One that interposes between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them.
ANGEL, n. A spirit, or a spiritual intelligent being employed by God in the government of the world.
scriptures: Acts 7:53
Who have received the law by the disposition of angels, and have not kept it.
Acts 7:51
Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.
Galatians 3:19
Wherefore then serveth the law? It was added because of transgressions, till the seed should come to whom the promise was made; and it was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator.
Hebrews 2:2
For if the word spoken by angels was stedfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompence of reward;
corruption_summary: The angelic mediation of the law is either ignored or used to depreciate the law as second-rate revelation, when Scripture uses it to raise the stakes of disobedience.
corruption_paragraphs: Because Galatians says the law was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator, some readers have concluded that the Sinai legislation is a lower order of revelation, given at a distance, perhaps not quite God's own word. Stephen and the writer to the Hebrews draw the opposite conclusion from the same fact. The word spoken by angels was stedfast; every transgression received a just recompence; and Israel, having received the law by the disposition of angels, had not kept it. The mediation magnifies the majesty of the giving. It never diminishes the authority of what was given.

The live misuse in the church is a practical antinomianism that treats the moral law as an expired arrangement rather than the abiding expression of God's character. The 1689 Confession is careful here: the ceremonial law is abrogated, the judicial law expired with that state, and the moral law binds all men for ever, believers not excepted. Stephen's charge was not that his hearers held the wrong theory of the law but that they had not kept it, and that their fathers had resisted the Spirit in exactly the same way. The argument from greater dignity to greater accountability falls hardest on those who have heard most.
roots_summary: Greek diatage (G1296), a disposition or ordinance; diatasso (G1299), to arrange; nomos (G3551), law; mesites (G3316), a mediator.
roots_lines: Greek diatage (G1296) — an arranging, disposition; Acts 7:53, by the disposition of angels.
Greek diatasso (G1299) — to set in order, appoint; the verb behind the noun.
Greek diatasso in Galatians 3:19 — ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator.
Greek mesites (G3316) — a mediator; Moses at Sinai, Christ in the new covenant.
Greek bebaios (G949) — stedfast, firm; the word spoken by angels, Hebrews 2:2.
usage: “Received the law by the disposition of angels” — Stephen's closing charge.
“Ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator” — Paul on the same delivery.
“How shall we escape, if we neglect” — the argument from dignity to accountability.

pos: v. (signed one's name beneath a written instrument)
etymology: From the Latin subscribere, to write underneath. Jeremiah uses it of the signature he put to a deed of purchase — the most improbable real-estate transaction in Scripture.
biblical_def: Jerusalem is under siege, the prophet is in prison for saying the city will fall, and God tells him to buy a field. He does it with every legal formality: “And I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it, and took witnesses, and weighed him the money in the balances” (Jeremiah 32:10). The deed is then handed over for safekeeping: “And I gave the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Hanameel mine uncle's son, and in the presence of the witnesses that subscribed the book of the purchase, before all the Jews that sat in the court of the prison” (Jeremiah 32:12). Baruch is instructed to store the documents for a long time: “Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days” (Jeremiah 32:14). And the reason is given plainly: “For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land” (Jeremiah 32:15). The signature was a sermon. A man who believes the exile is real and the return is certain buys land he will never farm and files the paperwork.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subscribe as to sign with one's own hand; to give consent to something written, by underwriting the name.
webster_full: SUBSCRIBE, v.t. To sign with one's own hand; to give consent to something written, by underwriting the name.
SUBSCRIBED, pp. Having the name written underneath; attested by writing the name.
EVIDENCE, n. That which elucidates and enables the mind to see truth; in law, a writing or deed proving a fact.
SEAL, n. A piece of metal or other hard substance, on which is engraved some image or device, used to make an impression on wax; that which confirms or ratifies.
REDEEM, v.t. To purchase back; to ransom; to liberate or rescue from captivity or bondage.
scriptures: Jeremiah 32:10
And I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it, and took witnesses, and weighed him the money in the balances.
Jeremiah 32:12

And I gave the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Hanameel mine uncle's son, and in the presence of the witnesses that subscribed the book of the purchase, before all the Jews that sat in the court of the prison.
Jeremiah 32:14

Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days.
Jeremiah 32:15
For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land.
corruption_summary: Faith is reduced to an inward attitude with no outward cost, whereas Jeremiah's belief in a promise was recorded on a deed, sealed, witnessed, and paid for in weighed silver.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that biblical faith characteristically takes a form that can be inspected. Jeremiah did not report a conviction that God would restore Judah; he weighed out seventeen shekels, signed a deed, sealed it, gathered witnesses, and had the documents archived in a clay jar for a future nobody in the besieged city could see. Hebrews 11 is a catalogue of exactly this: Noah built, Abraham went out, Moses refused, Joseph gave commandment concerning his bones. Where faith never becomes an act with a cost attached, Scripture does not recognise it.

There is a second lesson in the paperwork that the church has often needed. The prophet who bought the field is the same prophet who had announced the city's destruction and been imprisoned for it. He did not soften the judgment in order to hold the hope, and he did not abandon the hope because the judgment was certain. Both were the word of the LORD, and he acted on both in the same week. Preaching that can only say one or the other — only the coming reckoning, or only the coming restoration — has less than Jeremiah had in the court of the prison.
roots_summary: Hebrew kathab (H3789), to write; sepher (H5612), a book, deed or scroll; chatham (H2856), to seal; ed (H5707), a witness.
roots_lines: Hebrew kathab (H3789) — to write, subscribe; Jeremiah 32:10, I subscribed the evidence.
Hebrew sepher (H5612) — a writing, book, deed; the evidence of the purchase.
Hebrew chatham (H2856) — to seal, affix a seal; the sealed copy of the deed.
Hebrew ed (H5707) — a witness; those who subscribed the book of the purchase.

“Put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days” — filed for the return.
“Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again” — the promise purchased against.

etymology: From the Latin licentia, leave, from licet, it is permitted. Both occurrences are in Acts, and both concern a Roman officer granting a prisoner the right to speak.
biblical_def: Paul, seized in the temple and taken into custody, asks the chief captain for leave to address the crowd: “And when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue” (Acts 21:40). The second use states the Roman legal principle that kept Paul alive through the rest of the book: “To whom I answered, It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face, and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him” (Acts 25:16). Festus is explaining to Agrippa why he would not hand Paul over to the Sanhedrin. The apostle's own account of the same protection is his appeal: “I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged: to the Jews have I done no wrong, as thou very well knowest” (Acts 25:10). Providence used a pagan procedural rule to carry the gospel to Rome, and Paul says as much of his imprisonment: “But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel” (Philippians 1:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines licence as leave; permission; authority or liberty given to do or forbear any act.
webster_full: LICENSE, n. Leave; permission; authority or liberty given to do or forbear any act.
LICENSE, n. Excess of liberty; exorbitant freedom; freedom abused, or used in contempt of law or decorum.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
ACCUSER, n. One who accuses or blames; an officer who prefers a charge against a person.
APPEAL, n. The removal of a cause from an inferior to a superior tribunal.
scriptures: Acts 21:40
And when he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs, and beckoned with the hand unto the people. And when there was made a great silence, he spake unto them in the Hebrew tongue, saying,
Acts 25:16

To whom I answered, It is not the manner of the Romans to deliver any man to die, before that he which is accused have the accusers face to face , and have licence to answer for himself concerning the crime laid against him.
Acts 25:10
Then said Paul, I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged: to the Jews have I done no wrong, as thou very well knowest.
Philippians 1:12
But I would ye should understand, brethren, that the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel;
corruption_summary: The word has drifted from permission formally granted to liberty without restraint, and the modern sense is read back into a Bible that never uses it that way.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster already recorded both senses in 1828: licence as leave granted, and licence as liberty abused. English has since let the second sense swallow the first, so that a modern reader meets licence and hears permissiveness. Scripture uses only the first. In Acts the word describes a Roman officer granting a prisoner the right to speak — an act of lawful authority, carefully bounded, which the prisoner then uses. The distinction matters because the two senses are moral opposites: one is liberty under authority, the other liberty against it.

The theological application is the one Peter makes when he warns against using liberty for a cloke of maliciousness, and Jude when he describes men turning the grace of God into lasciviousness. Christian freedom in the Reformed confessions is always freedom granted — freedom from the curse of the law, from the dominion of sin, from the tyranny of men's consciences — and never freedom from the moral law as a rule of life. A believer who reasons from grace to permission has taken the word in the wrong sense, and Acts shows him the right one: leave given by a rightful authority, for a purpose, and answerable to the one who gave it.
roots_summary: Greek epitrepo (G2010), to permit or give leave; topos apologias, place of defence; apologeomai (G626), to answer for oneself; parresia (G3954), boldness of speech.
roots_lines: Greek epitrepo (G2010) — to turn over to, permit; Acts 21:40, when he had given him licence.
Greek apologia (G627) — a defence, verbal answer; the right Festus describes.
Greek apologeomai (G626) — to answer for oneself concerning a charge.
Greek parresia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech; how Paul used the leave granted.
Greek prokope (G4297) — furtherance, advance; Philippians 1:12, the gospel advanced by the arrest.
usage: “When he had given him licence, Paul stood on the stairs” — leave to address the crowd.
“Have licence to answer for himself” — the Roman rule Festus cites.
“Unto the furtherance of the gospel” — what providence made of the custody.

pos: n. (one who lends at interest, especially to the poor)
etymology: From the Latin usura, use or interest paid for money. The word occurs once, in the covenant code, where Israel is forbidden to stand in that relation to a poor brother.
biblical_def: The statute is addressed to the lender and defines him by how he treats the borrower: “If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury” (Exodus 22:25). The prohibition is not against lending; it is against a particular posture toward a particular borrower — a poor brother within the covenant community. The next verses show how far the protection extends, down to a garment taken in pledge: “If thou at all take thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, thou shalt deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down: for that is his covering only, it is his raiment for his skin: wherein shall he sleep?” (Exodus 22:26-27). Leviticus restates the rule and grounds it in the exodus: “Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee” (Leviticus 25:36). The Psalmist makes the practice a mark of the man who may dwell in God's holy hill: “He that putteth not out his money to usury, nor taketh reward against the innocent. He that doeth these things shall never be moved” (Psalm 15:5). The law never treats a poor man's need as a market opportunity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines usurer as one who lends money and takes interest for it; in a modern sense, one who takes exorbitant interest.
webster_full: USURER, n. One who lends money and takes interest for it; in present usage, one who exacts an exorbitant price for the use of money.
USURY, n. Formerly, interest; a premium paid for the use of money. In present usage, unlawful interest; a premium exceeding the rate established by law.
PLEDGE, n. Something put in pawn; that which is deposited with another as security for the repayment of money borrowed.
INCREASE, n. Addition; augmentation; profit; interest on money lent.
NEIGHBOR, n. One who lives near another; in Scripture, any one whom we may benefit.
scriptures: Exodus 22:25
If thou lend money to any of my people that is poor by thee, thou shalt not be to him as an usurer, neither shalt thou lay upon him usury.
Exodus 22:26
If thou at all take thy neighbour's raiment to pledge, thou shalt deliver it unto him by that the sun goeth down:
Leviticus 25:36
Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee.
Psalm 15:5
He that putteth not out his money to usury, nor taketh reward against the innocent. He that doeth these things shall never be moved.
corruption_summary: The statute is either dismissed as obsolete economics or stretched into a blanket condemnation of all lending at interest, and in both cases the poor brother the law was written to protect drops out of view.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite errors attend this law. The first treats it as a relic of a pre-commercial society with nothing to say now, since the modern economy runs on interest. The second, older and often sincere, reads it as forbidding interest absolutely, a position much of the medieval church held and which the Reformers re-examined. Calvin's judgment is the careful one: the law addresses a lender and a poor brother, its stated aim is that thy brother may live with thee, and the sin it names is the use of a neighbour's desperation as a source of increase. A commercial loan between parties who both profit is not the transaction Exodus 22 has in view.

What both errors lose is the person the statute protects. The chapter descends to the level of a cloak taken in pledge and insists it be returned before sundown because the man has nothing else to sleep in. That is the register of the whole law: God hears the cry of the poor, and He tells the lender so directly — when he crieth unto me, I will hear; for I am gracious. The biblical categories here are the poor, the widow, the fatherless and the stranger, each with a claim God Himself enforces. Any reading of this statute that ends without those people in it has missed the law.

“He that putteth not out his money to usury” — a mark of the man in Psalm 15.

pos: adv. (with reproach; in a manner conveying contempt)
etymology: From reproach, Old French reprocher, to cast back in one's teeth. It occurs twice: of Job's tormentors, and of the occasion a careless household gives an adversary.
biblical_def: Job describes what his comforters have become: “They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me” (Job 16:10). The blow to the cheek is contempt made physical, and the word marks the manner rather than the injury. Paul uses the adverb in a directive about household order: “I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully” (1 Timothy 5:14). The concern is the mouth of an opponent, and the apostle assumes that conduct in a Christian home is being watched and will be spoken of. He states the same principle for servants: “Let as many servants as are under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honour, that the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed” (1 Timothy 6:1). And Peter grounds the whole concern in what God does with such conduct: “Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation” (1 Peter 2:12). Reproach against the church, when it is deserved, falls on the doctrine and on the Name.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reproach as censure mingled with contempt or derision; and reproachfully as in a manner conveying reproach or contempt.
webster_full: REPROACH, v.t. To censure with severity, or with contemptuous language; to upbraid.
REPROACHFULLY, adv. In terms of reproach; opprobriously; with contempt; shamefully.
ADVERSARY, n. An enemy or foe; one who opposes another in a suit at law.
BLASPHEME, v.t. To speak of the Supreme Being in terms of impious irreverence; to revile or speak reproachfully of God.
CONVERSATION, n. In Scripture, general course of manners; behavior; deportment.
scriptures: They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me.
1 Timothy 5:14
I will therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, guide the house, give none occasion to the adversary to speak reproachfully.
1 Timothy 6:1
Let as many servants as are under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honour, that the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed.
1 Peter 2:12
Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.
corruption_summary: Concern for the church's reputation is dismissed as people-pleasing, or else inflated until avoiding criticism becomes the governing rule of Christian conduct.
corruption_paragraphs: One error treats Paul's concern about giving the adversary occasion as mere respectability — a first-century preoccupation with appearances that a bolder faith would shrug off. The apostles do not shrug it off. They tie the church's conduct directly to whether the name of God and His doctrine are blasphemed, which makes it a matter of the third commandment rather than of public relations. What outsiders say about a household or a congregation attaches, in Scripture's reckoning, to the God whose name it bears.

The opposite error makes the avoidance of reproach into the supreme rule, so that whatever the world finds offensive is quietly dropped. That is not what Paul asks. He asks for conduct that gives no occasion — that is, that the reproach, when it comes, should be a lie. Peter assumes it will come anyway: they speak against you as evildoers. Christ promised as much. The distinction the church must keep is between reproach earned by sin, which dishonours God, and reproach earned by fidelity, which Scripture calls blessed. Job's tormentors smote him reproachfully, and God said at the end that Job had spoken rightly.
roots_summary: Hebrew cherpah (H2781), reproach, disgrace; Greek loidoria (G3059), reviling; antikeimenos (G480), the adversary; blasphemeo (G987), to speak evil of.

Greek loidoria (G3059) — reviling, abuse; occasion to speak reproachfully, 1 Timothy 5:14.
Greek antikeimai (G480) — to be an adversary, to oppose; the one watching the household.

Greek anastrophe (G391) — manner of life, conversation; 1 Peter 2:12.

“Give none occasion to the adversary” — the apostolic charge to households.
“That the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed” — what is at stake.

pos: n. (reasoning; the case a man makes in debate)
etymology: From the Latin arguere, to make clear, to prove. The word occurs once, in Job's reply to Eliphaz, and it draws the sharpest distinction in the book between speech that is true and speech that convicts.
biblical_def: Job answers his friend with a sentence that has never lost its edge: “How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?” (Job 6:25). He concedes the power of true speech and denies that his friends have produced any. The complaint continues: “Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind?” (Job 6:26). They have been correcting his phrasing while ignoring his condition. Job then names what a friend owes a sufferer: “To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty” (Job 6:14). The book vindicates this complaint at its close, when God addresses Eliphaz directly: “My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath” (Job 42:7). The friends' arguing was orthodox in form — God is just, the wicked suffer, therefore repent — and God calls it wrong speech about Himself. Right words are forcible; arguing that reproves nothing is only noise, however sound its propositions look on the page.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines arguing as reasoning; discussing; evincing; disputing; and to argue as to offer reasons to support an opinion.
webster_full: ARGUE, v.i. To reason; to invent and offer reasons to support or overthrow a proposition, opinion or measure.
ARGUING, ppr. Inventing and offering reasons; disputing; discussing; evincing; persuading.
REPROVE, v.t. To blame; to censure; to charge with a fault to the face; to convince of a fault.
FORCIBLE, a. Powerful; strong; efficacious; impressive; having power to persuade.
COMFORTER, n. One who administers comfort or consolation; one who strengthens and supports the mind in distress.
scriptures: Job 6:25
How forcible are right words! but what doth your arguing reprove?
Job 6:26
Do ye imagine to reprove words, and the speeches of one that is desperate, which are as wind?
Job 6:14
To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed from his friend; but he forsaketh the fear of the Almighty.
Job 42:7

And it was so, that after the LORD had spoken these words unto Job, the LORD said to Eliphaz the Temanite, My wrath is kindled against thee, and against thy two friends: for ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.
corruption_summary: Doctrinal correctness is treated as sufficient warrant for any speech, when God Himself judged the friends' arguing wrong though their propositions were largely orthodox.
corruption_paragraphs: The friends of Job are the standing warning against a particular error that orthodox men are most liable to: assembling true statements into a false accusation. God is just; God does not afflict without cause; therefore the afflicted man has a cause to confess. Each premise is defensible; the conclusion crushed an innocent man; and the LORD said plainly they had not spoken of Him the thing that was right. Doctrine can be handled so as to misrepresent the God it describes. That is the whole burden of Job 6:25 — right words are forcible, and your arguing reproves nothing.

The contemporary corruption runs in both directions. On one side, a therapeutic instinct concludes from this chapter that doctrine should be withheld from sufferers altogether and replaced with presence and sympathy — which is not what Job asks for; he asks for right words, and he asks God for answers to the last page. On the other side stands the counsellor who deploys texts at a grieving man as a solution to be applied. Job names the alternative to both in verse 14: pity should be shewed from his friend. Pity and truth are not rivals in Scripture. In the friends they came apart, and God rebuked what was left.

“What doth your arguing reprove?” — and denies his friends have used it.
“Ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right” — God's verdict on the debate.

etymology: From the Latin obscurus, dark, covered. The one occurrence pairs it with darkness to intensify it — obscure darkness, a blackness beyond ordinary night — as the end of the lamp of the man who curses his parents.
biblical_def: The proverb is one of the severest in the book: “Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness” (Proverbs 20:20). The lamp in Proverbs is the ongoing life of a house — its continuance, its name, its light in the window — and the sentence is that it goes out, and goes out into a darkness the writer has to double the words to describe. The law had made the same judgment without metaphor: “And he that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death” (Exodus 21:17). The Lord Jesus cites that very statute against a tradition that had found a way around it: “For God commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death” (Matthew 15:4). And the positive form of the commandment carries the first promise attached to any: “Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee” (Exodus 20:12). Long days for the honouring child; a lamp put out in obscure darkness for the cursing one. Scripture sets the fifth commandment at the foundation of the second table and does not treat contempt for parents as a private family matter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines obscure as dark; destitute of light; and figuratively, not easily understood, or living in darkness.
webster_full: OBSCURE, a. Dark; destitute of light; as the obscure night.
OBSCURITY, n. Darkness; want of light; a state of retirement from the world; a state of being unknown.
LAMP, n. A vessel with a wick, used with oil to furnish artificial light; in Scripture, a figure of life and posterity.
CURSE, v.t. To utter a wish of evil against one; to imprecate evil upon; to blaspheme.
HONOR, v.t. To revere; to respect; to treat with deference and submission, and perform relative duties to.
scriptures: Proverbs 20:20
Whoso curseth his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness.
Exodus 21:17
And he that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death.
Matthew 15:4
For God commanded, saying, Honour thy father and mother: and, He that curseth father or mother, let him die the death.
Exodus 20:12
Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
corruption_summary: The fifth commandment is reduced to a sentiment about family warmth, and a culture that treats contempt for parents as a stage of healthy development has no category for the proverb's severity.
corruption_paragraphs: Contempt for parents is now widely treated as a developmental phase, a necessary individuation, or the justified response of a wounded adult child. Scripture allows none of these as a general rule. The fifth commandment stands at the head of the second table, and its breach is punished in the law with death and in the Proverbs with a lamp put out in obscure darkness. The severity is not arbitrary. Parental authority is the first authority every human being meets, and a heart trained to despise it is being trained for every other rebellion, including the last one.

Scripture is not naive about bad parents. It commands fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, it records David's failures and Eli's, and it never requires obedience to a parent commanding sin. The Lord Jesus Himself, in the passage where He cites this statute, is rebuking men who used a religious device — declaring a gift Corban — to escape supporting their aged parents. That is the exact modern temptation in an older costume: finding a principled-sounding reason to withhold honour that is owed. The command survives the parent's failures because it rests on God's ordering of the family, not on the parent's merit.
roots_summary: Hebrew ishun (H380), the blackest part of night; choshek (H2822), darkness; ner (H5216), a lamp; qalal (H7043), to curse or make light of.
roots_lines: Hebrew ishun (H380) — the pupil of the eye, hence the blackest hour; obscure darkness.
Hebrew choshek (H2822) — darkness; doubled with ishun for intensity in Proverbs 20:20.
Hebrew ner (H5216) — a lamp; in Proverbs, the life and continuance of a house.
Hebrew qalal (H7043) — to make light of, curse, treat with contempt.
Hebrew kabad (H3513) — to be heavy, to honour; the verb of the fifth commandment.
usage: “His lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness” — the end of the cursing child.
“He that curseth his father, or his mother, shall surely be put to death” — the law behind it.
“That thy days may be long upon the land” — the promise on the other side.

pos: adj. (wavering; unsettled; of a mind held in suspense)
etymology: From doubt, Latin dubitare, to waver. Both New Testament uses concern a mind suspended — over food and tomorrow in Luke, over disputable matters in Romans.
biblical_def: Our Lord forbids a particular kind of mental suspension: “And seek not ye what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink, neither be ye of doubtful mind” (Luke 12:29). The Greek behind doubtful mind pictures a ship riding high and unsettled, and the cure He gives is not effort but knowledge of the Father: “For all these things do the nations of the world seek after: and your Father knoweth that ye have need of these things” (Luke 12:30). Paul uses the word of a different suspense — the disputed questions that divide congregations: “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (Romans 14:1). The weaker brother is to be welcomed, not enrolled in an argument about his scruples. Paul then gives the rule that governs the whole chapter: “And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Romans 14:23). A man must not act against his own conscience even when his conscience is poorly informed; he must have it better informed first. Two texts, two different doubts — anxiety about provision and uncertainty about liberty — and in both the answer is a settled confidence: in the Father who knows, and in the Lord to whom every servant stands or falls.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines doubtful as dubious; not settled in opinion; undetermined; wavering; hesitating.
webster_full: DOUBTFUL, a. Dubious; not settled in opinion; undetermined; wavering; hesitating.
DOUBT, v.i. To waver or fluctuate in opinion; to hesitate; to be in suspense.
DISPUTATION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
SCRUPLE, n. Doubt; hesitation from the difficulty of determining what is right.
scriptures: Luke 12:29
And seek not ye what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink, neither be ye of doubtful mind.
Luke 12:30
For all these things do the nations of the world seek after: and your Father knoweth that ye have need of these things.
Romans 14:1
Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
Romans 14:23
And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
corruption_summary: Doubt is promoted from a condition to be cured into a virtue to be cultivated, and a chapter written to protect the weak conscience is used to make uncertainty itself the mark of an honest faith.
corruption_paragraphs: A considerable strand of modern religious writing treats doubt as the more honest posture and certainty as arrogance — faith redefined as a comfort with unanswered questions. Scripture does not flatter doubt. James says the wavering man is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed, and must not think he shall receive anything of the Lord. Our Lord treats the doubtful mind as a symptom of not knowing the Father well enough, and prescribes knowledge rather than resignation. Honest questions are everywhere in the Bible — the Psalms are full of them — but they are always addressed to God and always press toward an answer.

Romans 14 is meanwhile put to a use Paul never intended, as a general instruction to treat contested doctrines as matters of indifference. The chapter is about meat, drink and holy days — genuinely indifferent things — and its ruling principle is that a man must not violate his own conscience. Paul had no such tolerance for the Galatian error or the Corinthian denial of the resurrection; on those he was immovable. Wisdom lies in telling the two categories apart, and a church that files justification under doubtful disputations has not learned charity. It has lost the faith it was charitable about.

“Not to doubtful disputations” — how the weak brother is received.
“Whatsoever is not of faith is sin” — the rule for a scrupled conscience.

pos: v. (engaged or occupied in a work)
etymology: From the French employer, to use or occupy. Both occurrences describe men set to a defined task — the temple singers on continuous duty, and two men assigned to a difficult matter in Ezra.
biblical_def: The Chronicler records an arrangement that assumes worship never stops: “And these are the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites, who remaining in the chambers were free: for they were employed in that work day and night” (1 Chronicles 9:33). They were free — released from other Levitical duties — precisely because this one occupied them entirely. The second use is in Ezra, where a contested question is handed to named men: “Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahaziah the son of Tikvah were employed about this matter: and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them” (Ezra 10:15). Work in Scripture is characteristically assigned, named and accountable. The pattern goes back to the garden: “And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it” (Genesis 2:15) — labour before the fall, given as a charge rather than imposed as a curse. And the New Testament carries the same principle into every occupation a believer may hold: “And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Colossians 3:23). The singers employed day and night and the men employed about a hard matter are doing the same kind of thing: a task set by God, discharged before Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines employ as to occupy the time, attention and labor of; to keep busy, or at work; and employed as occupied or used.
webster_full: EMPLOY, v.t. To occupy the time, attention and labor of; to keep busy, or at work; to use.
EMPLOYED, pp. Occupied; used; engaged in a particular business or service.
VOCATION, n. Calling; employment; profession; business; the calling of a man to the Christian faith.
CALLING, n. A proper station or employment; the occupation in which a man is engaged.
DILIGENCE, n. Steady application in business of any kind; constant effort to accomplish what is undertaken.
scriptures: 1 Chronicles 9:33
And these are the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites, who remaining in the chambers were free : for they were employed in that work day and night.
Ezra 10:15
Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahaziah the son of Tikvah were employed about this matter: and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them.
Genesis 2:15
And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
Colossians 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily , as to the Lord, and not unto men;
corruption_summary: Work is split into sacred and secular tiers, so that the singer in the temple is thought to serve God and the man at an ordinary trade merely to earn a living.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the Reformation doctrine of vocation. Medieval Christendom graded labour, with contemplative and priestly work at the top and common trades beneath, and the Reformers dismantled the ladder from Scripture: whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord. The Levitical singers employed day and night were doing holy work, and so was the man at the plough, because holiness is determined by the God who assigns the task and the faith in which it is done, not by the material handled.

The modern form of the same error is subtler and runs the other way. Work is now widely treated as the primary source of identity and meaning, and a man's employment is asked to supply what only God can give. Scripture sets labour before the fall — Adam dressed and kept a garden in innocence — so work is good and original, not a punishment. But the man in the garden was a steward under a Lord, and the labour had a Sabbath built around it. An employment that recognises no Sabbath and no Master has become the thing it was meant to serve.
